Stepwells of India: baolis and vavs, how they worked

By @archaeologywala for Talaash Heritage · Updated 15 October 2026

A stepwell is a well reached by a long flight of steps that lead down through several storeys to groundwater. Known as baoli or baori in north India and vav in Gujarat, stepwells stored water through dry months and served as cool public spaces. Famous examples include Rani-ki-Vav at Patan, Chand Baori at Abhaneri and Agrasen ki Baoli in Delhi.

Talaash Heritage runs short walks at Agrasen ki Baoli and Rajon ki Baoli in Delhi for schools, families and photography groups.

What is a stepwell?

In much of western and northern India, rain falls in a few monsoon months and the rest of the year is dry. Groundwater can drop many metres. A stepwell solves this by cutting a deep trench down to the water table and lining it with steps and landings, so people can walk down to the water at whatever level it stands.

A typical stepwell has two parts: a vertical well shaft at one end, from which water could be drawn up by rope, and a long stepped corridor leading down to it, often roofed by pillared pavilions at each level. The pavilions shaded the steps, kept the water cool and gave space for rest, gossip and ritual.

Names vary by region. In Gujarat they are vav; in Rajasthan and Hindi-speaking regions, baori or baoli. Large stepped tanks with steps on all sides, such as the kunds of Rajasthan and the temple tanks of the south, are close relatives.

History of stepwells in India

Stepped access to water has a long history in India. The great reservoirs and stepped cuttings at Dholavira show Harappan water engineering, though the classic stepwell form developed much later. Rock-cut stepped wells and ponds appear in the early centuries CE, and the building type flourished from around the 7th century onward.

The peak came between about the 11th and 16th centuries in Gujarat and Rajasthan, when queens, merchants and rulers paid for stepwells as acts of charity and prestige. Sultanate and Mughal builders adopted the form too, and Delhi has several. Under British rule many stepwells were filled in or neglected as piped water and tube wells spread, and only in recent decades have many been cleaned and protected.

Delhi's stepwells are easy to reach. A walk to Agrasen ki Baoli takes an hour in central Delhi, and a Rajon ki Baoli focus walk sits inside the Mehrauli Archaeological Park.

Stepwell architecture: how to read one

Walk down slowly and look at the structure as engineering first. Notice how each landing is braced by pillars and beams across the trench, holding back the earth on both sides. That repeated bracing is what gives a stepwell its rhythm of frames and shadows.

Then look at the water level marks, steps worn smooth in the middle, and the small niches that once held lamps or images. In Gujarat vavs, sculpture can be dense: Rani-ki-Vav has rows of deities, apsaras and scenes that rival a temple. In Sultanate and Mughal stepwells, decoration is plainer, with arches and rubble masonry finished in plaster.

Stepwells are one part of India's long tradition of water architecture, alongside tanks, dams and canals. A visit to Mandu's fortified plateau and water architecture and the Satpula waterworks in Delhi show other solutions to the same problem.

Visiting stepwells: practical tips

  • Steps are steep, worn and often without railings. Wear shoes with grip and keep children close.
  • Early morning or late afternoon light is best for photographs down the shaft.
  • Several are protected monuments; check the ASI or state department website before you go for timings.
  • Do not throw coins or rubbish into the water, a common cause of damage.

Stepwells of India: notes for students

  • Definition: a well with steps leading down to groundwater, often several storeys deep.
  • Regional names: vav (Gujarat), baori or baoli (Rajasthan, north India).
  • Main period of building: about the 11th to 16th centuries in Gujarat and Rajasthan.
  • Rani-ki-Vav, Patan: built in the 11th century, linked to Queen Udayamati; UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014.
  • Delhi examples: Agrasen ki Baoli, Rajon ki Baoli, Gandhak ki Baoli.

Questions people ask

What is a stepwell called in India?

A stepwell is called a baoli or baori in Hindi-speaking north India and Rajasthan, and a vav in Gujarat. Related stepped tanks are called kund, and in south India temple tanks are often called kulam or pushkarini.

Which is the most famous stepwell in India?

Rani-ki-Vav at Patan in Gujarat is the best known. Built in the 11th century under the Chaulukya (Solanki) dynasty, it is richly carved with sculpture and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2014. Chand Baori at Abhaneri in Rajasthan is also very famous.

Why were stepwells built?

To reach groundwater that rose and fell with the seasons in dry regions. Steps let people walk down to the water at any level. Stepwells also gave cool shaded spaces for rest and social gathering, and building one was seen as an act of charity.

How many stepwells are there in Delhi?

Delhi has more than a dozen surviving stepwells, of which Agrasen ki Baoli, Rajon ki Baoli and Gandhak ki Baoli in Mehrauli, and the baolis at the Red Fort and Purana Qila, are among the best known. Exact counts vary by source.
